clips.text: A junctional rhythm begins in or near the A V junction. Activation may travel normally toward the ventricles and backward toward the atria. Retrograde P waves may be inverted in inferior leads, appear before or after the Q R S, or be hidden within it. If a retrograde P wave precedes the Q R S, the P R interval is often short. Surface timing alone does not precisely locate the focus within an upper, middle, or lower node.

clips.text: A premature junctional complex is an early beat arising from the A V junction. Its Q R S is usually narrow if ventricular conduction is normal. A retrograde P wave may be visible before or after the complex, or may be hidden. Compare the beat with the expected timing of the underlying rhythm. Prematurity distinguishes it from a junctional escape beat, which arrives late after a pause or slowing of higher pacemakers.

clips.text: A junctional escape rhythm is usually taught at forty to sixty beats per minute. An accelerated junctional rhythm is around sixty to one hundred, and junctional tachycardia is faster than one hundred. Boundaries vary among references. These names combine origin and rate; they do not by themselves describe the person's circulation. Atrial and ventricular timing can vary, and a one-to-one atrial-ventricular relationship is not guaranteed in every junctional rhythm.

clips.text: Supraventricular tachycardia is a broad category of tachycardias involving tissue above the ventricles, including several different mechanisms. In bedside shorthand, S V T often means a regular narrow-complex tachycardia whose exact mechanism is not yet clear. That shorthand is not the entire formal definition. Some supraventricular rhythms can be irregular, and aberrant conduction can make them wide. Describe the rhythm before assuming a specific mechanism.

clips.text: Rates overlap among sinus tachycardia, atrial tachycardia, flutter with conduction, and re-entry tachycardias. Hidden P waves make identification harder. Compare regularity, atrial activity, Q R S shape, and any documented onset or termination. This lesson deliberately does not reproduce the audiobook's medication dose or cardioversion sequence. Those are clinical actions requiring current protocols, trained judgment, and information that a website strip alone cannot supply.
